title: The opening greeting
hookLine: it begins with Ik Onkar and the Khalsa's greeting to Waheguru

lines: A FEW WORDS, AND THEY KNOW.
cards: Two Sikhs meet at an airport, strangers, and one says: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. The other answers right away: Waheguru ji ki fateh. They've never met, but in a handful of words they've placed each other.
It's the Khalsa's greeting, which Sikh tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh, used at the start of a speech, the end of a letter, the top of a wedding card.
Half of it, with one small symbol in front, is also how the Ardas begins. Before the prayer remembers anyone or asks for anything, it says who the victory belongs to.

teach.b: The Ardas opens: Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Ik Onkar is the very first word of the Guru Granth Sahib: the numeral one joined to the sign for Onkar. One God, everywhere, flowing through everything.
Then Waheguru, the wondrous Guru, a name for God. Ji is respect, like saying sir or dear.
And fateh is victory. The grammar is worth a second look. Waheguru ji ki fateh doesn't quite say victory to Waheguru, like a cheer.
It says the victory is Waheguru's: the victory belongs to God. The first half of the full greeting says the same about the community: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru.
So the line often rendered victory to Waheguru carries the sense that the victory is already Waheguru's. The greeting hands everything over.
The community isn't ours; it's God's.
The victory isn't ours; it's God's. Putting it at the head of the Ardas does the same work.

Whatever the prayer goes on to ask, a good marriage, a safe flight, a recovery, the first thing said is: if anything goes well, the victory is God's. That takes some weight off. It also takes some pride off.
The same heading, Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, stands at the top of Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, where the Ardas's next lines come from.
So the greeting is like the letterhead on a page: the first thing you see, telling you whose house you're in.

how: The Ardas begins with Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, and Sikhs greet one another with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, at meetings, in speeches and in letters.

o: a vow taken at the Khalsa initiation
a welcome given to a guest at the door

games.q: the opening greeting — tap the pairs.

s: Waheguru ji ki fateh means the victory belongs to Waheguru
ki makes it possessive: the victory is God's.
the Ardas opens with a request
it opens with Ik Onkar and the greeting, before anything is asked.
the Khalsa greeting is only used in the gurdwara
it's used at meetings, in speeches, at the end of letters.

games.q: a stranger at the airport says to you: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. what's the answer?
games.why: the greeting has two halves: the Khalsa is Waheguru's, and the victory is Waheguru's. the second half also opens the Ardas.

practice: Sit or stand comfortably, and say the words slowly, aloud or silently, a few times: Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Each time, notice what you're handing over: whatever goes well today, the victory isn't yours to carry.
If you don't pray, sit with the idea instead: a success that doesn't need your pride.

wordCard.voice: Fateh, victory. Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh: one God everywhere, and the fateh belongs to the wondrous Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fateh, victory; in Waheguru ji ki fateh, the victory belongs to God.

carryVoice: Your line: victory to waheguru. The credit goes where the victory belongs. Day six hundred twelve.
